item.title: Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2rzxrdr71o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne - Published Norwegians are grieving the death of the beloved King Harald V, as a period of national mourning begins and his son Haakon VIII assumes the throne. After Harald's death was announced early on Friday, crowds amassed at the royal palace in Oslo, laying flowers and flags, some mourners visibly in tears. The 53-year-old new king held an extraordinary council of state meeting with government ministers, saying he was taking on the royal family's motto "All for Norway". Harald - who was on the throne for 35 years - died in hospital at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) aged 89, after being treated there for a rare blood condition. His coffin was later taken to the palace in a public procession. An estimated 10,000 people lined the streets in the capital to see the late king go past, Norway's public broadcaster reported. The late monarch has been described as an inclusive, transparent and empathetic "people's king" who modernised the Norwegian monarchy. European royals, including King Charles III - whose mother Queen Elizabeth II was Harald's second cousin - as well as political leaders and ordinary citizens, paid tribute to his service and the stability he brought to the country. Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude". In a televised memorial address - one of multiple eulogies by ministers - he said the late king's "legacy lives on" and offered condolences to the royal family and Queen Sonja, who would have celebrated her 58th wedding anniversary with Harald on Saturday. Norway's superstar footballer Erling Haaland thanked Harald for "everything you meant to Norway" in a post on Instagram, adding that it had been an honour to meet him earlier in the summer at the palace following the Fifa World Cup. In the country's capital, Norwegians shared their grief and affection for the late king. "I personally will say he was everything for us, especially being an immigrant," Biteya Terfassa, an Oslo resident who was born in Ethiopia, told news agency Reuters outside the palace. "He made us feel at home and he made us feel loved. So he was like a grandfather that I never had." At noon, the Norwegian Armed Forces honoured Harald with a funeral salute of 21 shots from Akershus Fortress in central Oslo. Later on Friday, a procession left the chapel at Rikshospitalet, where Harald died, taking his coffin in a hearse to the royal palace. The date of Harald's funeral is yet to be officially announced. Until then, he will be lying in state in the palace chapel so the public can pay their last respects. During the national mourning period, flags will be flown at half-mast across the Nordic country, while Harald's portrait will be displayed, candles lit and moments of silence held at professional events. All non work-related social events will be cancelled or postponed. Oslo Mayor Anne Lindboe, who was due to get married on Friday, even postponed her wedding. King Haakon, who is Harald's younger child, is now the monarch and his wife Mette-Marit queen. He is due to take an oath before the Norwegian parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service - a stripped-down version of a coronation, which Norway no longer has. His daughter, the 22-year-old Ingrid Alexandra, who joined her father to meet ministers at the palace on Friday, is next in line to the throne as crown princess after the rules of succession changed in 1990 to allow firstborn women to inherit the crown. Haakon assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year. Now-Queen Mette-Marit came under scrutiny earlier this year when it was revealed that she had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she has publicly apologised. Later in the year, she received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care. Meanwhile, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing. Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when now-King Haakon married his mother. Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year found that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%. However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges. - Published11 hours ago - Published12 hours ago - Published7 hours ago

item.title: Oslo mayor calls off wedding ceremony after death of Norway's king
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ydgk3v60eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Oslo mayor calls off wedding ceremony after death of Norway's king - Published Oslo's Mayor Anne Lindboe has called off her wedding ceremony because of the death of King Harald V of Norway. The wedding with her fiancé Pål Sandvid was planned to take place on Friday but was postponed after the king died earlier the same day, her political adviser confirmed to the BBC. "It's hard to imagine an Oslo and a Norway without you. You didn't need a crown to be king," Lindboe wrote in a tribute to the late monarch on Instagram. Harald reigned for 35 years and died at the national hospital in Norway's capital, where he was being treated for a rare blood condition. His son, King Haakon VIII, ascended the throne on Friday. - Who is Norway's new King Haakon VIII? - Published11 hours ago - Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises - Published12 hours ago "Even the majority of Norwegians who never met you in person still felt like they knew you," Lindboe added in her tribute. No new date has been set for the wedding yet, Lindboe's political adviser said. After five years together, Lindboe announced the couple's engagement in June this year. The late king was a popular and reforming leader in Norway who modernised the monarchy. He broke with tradition by marrying a commoner, Queen Sonja, and served as a unifying figure during Norway's most difficult moments. Harald died a day before their 58th wedding anniversary. Members of the public have been gathering to lay flowers at a memorial outside the Royal Palace in Oslo. Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a televised memorial address that his country was "united in grief and gratitude" for Harald's service and that his "legacy lives on". The UK's King Charles III said he was mourning his "dear cousin". King Harald V was a second cousin of the King's mother, Queen Elizabeth II. Haakon VIII is the great-great-great-grandson of Queen Victoria.

item.title: Russia ramps up rhetoric but wants to avoid war with Nato, Western officials say
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz0zm2j7ld1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Russia ramps up rhetoric but wants to avoid war with Nato, Western officials say - Published Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to avoid a direct military confrontation with Nato, despite increasingly hostile rhetoric aimed at the UK and other allies over their support for Ukraine, Western officials believe. Some reports have suggested the visit by CIA chief John Radcliffe to Moscow this week was, in part, to warn Russia against a possible attack on a member of the Euro-Atlantic military alliance. But the Western officials, who asked not to be named, said recent warnings from Moscow, including that UK forces could be targeted in future or that its weapons factories could be hit, were "nothing new". They were, they suggested, consistent with Russia's military doctrine to apply pressure on the West. The officials suggested that the hostile rhetoric was also a reflection of the growing pressure Putin is facing at home, with slow and costly gains in Ukraine along with the impact of Ukrainian long-range strikes deep inside Russia. Putin and his officials have repeatedly dismissed warnings of Russian plans to attack Nato countries as hysteria. And US President Donald Trump appears to believe the Russian leader – saying this week that "he's not going to attack a Nato territory". Not long before launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Putin had given public assurances that he had no intention of attacking Russia's neighbour - despite overwhelming US intelligence that such preparations were in full swing. However, the senior Western officials said on Friday that Russia would likely continue its "hybrid activity", short of direct military action, using methods such as cyber-attacks, sabotage and even assassination attempts. They said that was aimed at breaking Western resolve and support for Ukraine. One official highlighted the risks of that Russian strategy leading to a miscalculation -which could spark a military confrontation. Russia is suspected of being behind a string of recent drone incidents in several Nato countries. Earlier this month, a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway in Germany's Leipzig airport - a key logistics hub for transferring military equipment to Ukraine. There is no proof to link the incident directly to Russia, which has denied any role. It came amid a string of drone sightings over European airports and military bases that began last year and which are also suspected of being the work of Russia, though it again denies this. Following the Leipzig incident, the head of France's security services warned that "we must consider the possibility of direct, more violent hostile actions on our national soil". Still, one Western official said Nato allies should remain calm but not complacent. The UK government has already made clear that recent Russian threats will not deter its support for Ukraine. The Western officials said the Ukraine war had "escalated" this year, with both Moscow and Kyiv stepping up their own long-range strike campaigns. Putin, they said, had not changed his maximalist objectives, despite some signs of increasing frustrations back home. They said petrol shortages in Russia were having an impact on support for the war. They believed there was increasing political pressure on the Russian leader, but that this did not pose a critical challenge to his power. Russia is still making slow gains in the eastern Donbas region. But it's also facing heavy casualties. The officials said Russia was losing 6,000 more soldiers a month - either killed or wounded - than it can recruit. That said, there is no indication yet that the Kremlin leader will resort to mass mobilisation. Related topics - Published3 days ago - Published5 August - Published4 days ago

item.title: Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj06jgq62v9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE - Published British right-wing political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is awaiting deportation. Yiannopoulos, 41, a former editor of Breitbart News and onetime employee of rapper Kanye West, appears to be held in Louisiana, according to ICE's inmate registry. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said he "was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing", and will remain in custody pending deportation. The self-styled provocateur has called himself the "most fabulous supervillain on the internet". His critics call him a purveyor of hate speech. Yiannopoulos, who grew up in Kent in the south of England, was arrested on 27 August after arriving at the airport in New Orleans. He flew into the US in May 2019 and "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws", said DHS. The DHS statement referred to him as "an illegal alien from the United Kingdom". The BBC has asked the British embassy in Washington for comment. Yiannopoulos did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. "Being in detention is a choice," the DHS statement continued, calling on migrants who are in the US illegally to "self-deport now". Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 election, headlining an event that year called Gays for Trump during the Republican National Convention. But he soon fell out with the movement. Yiannopoulos still voices support for the Republican president's agenda. But he posted in March this year on X that Trump "has lost his way, bought off by foreign interests". Yiannopoulos has courted controversy with his comments on transgender people, Muslims, Black Lives Matter, feminists and gay people, even though he himself identified as gay. He now calls himself an "ex-gay". He has written columns titled "Birth Control Makes Women Unattractive and Crazy" and "Would You Rather Your Child Had Feminism or Cancer?" He has also cheered on ICE raids, writing on X last year: "Total legal immunity for ICE agents when they're on duty." He posted in 2025: "We have got to deport millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters." Yiannopoulos also advocated on social media for "on the spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they are in the US legally". In 2017, he was uninvited from speaking at CPAC, a US conservative conference that also hosted Trump, after footage emerged of Yiannopoulos appearing to condone paedophilia. He also later apologised and resigned from Breitbart. He denied the allegations, and said he had been speaking about his own experiences as a child. Yiannopoulos was once regularly linked with the alt-right, a disparate group that is outspoken against political correctness and feminism and which includes neo-Nazis and white supremacists. He has said he does not consider himself part of the alt-right, although he has called it "energising and exciting". Related topics - Published21 February 2017 - Published5 December 2017

item.title: Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers, mayor says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2q7gv3l5qo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers, mayor says - Published Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers who were able to compromise city systems and steal data earlier this month, its mayor has said. Kai Wegner said officials would not cave in to the ransom demand, which came on Thursday evening. He did not say how much was being sought, though Der Spiegel reports the hackers are demanding 30 bitcoin, worth around €2m (£1.7m). Some of the German capital's online systems were forced to close down as a result of the attack, while investigators were working to understand what data had been taken. The Rhysida group, which is thought to operate from Russia and eastern Europe, and was behind a previous attack on the British Museum, has reportedly taken responsibility. It has said on its website it intends to begin auctioning the 5.79 terabytes of data it was able to steal from Berlin in seven days' time, according to news agency Reuters. "Berlin will not be blackmailed," Wegner said on Friday. He said state police, prosecutors and federal security services were working to investigate the suspected perpetrators "with the utmost urgency", adding that inquiries into the "content and scope of the compromised data are being pursued with great intensity". Officials for the city-state said an initial data leak occurred between 7 and 12 August. Then, on 14 August, two department networks were shut down, making applications for housing benefits and payments impossible for several days. Forensic investigations had since revealed further data leaks within Berlin's transport and environment department, officials said. "It cannot be ruled out that personal or other non-public data may also be affected," the mayor's office said in a statement on Friday. Authorities in the capital have not named the suspected cyber-attackers, though Der Spiegel is carrying a screenshot of the Rhysida group's dark web site claiming to possess files including contracts, non-disclosure agreements, personnel files, passwords and thousands of personal contact details. It is also displaying a countdown, after which it says it will begin auctioning off the data with a starting price of 30 bitcoin - the same amount of the cryptocurrency being sought from Berlin, the German newspaper reports. The Rhysida group has claimed hundreds of attacks since it emerged in 2023, studies say, and the group has targeted government insititutions and businesses of varying sizes in numerous countries. It successfully infiltrated the British Museum's computer systems in 2023, disrupting services and stealing around 500,000 files. When the UK institution refused to pay the ransom, the group published the files - containing the personal data of visitors, subscribers and staff - on the dark web. The Berlin cyber-attack comes roughly a month before the city holds elections, though state senator Iris Spranger insisted that election infrastructure had not been compromised. item.title: Thieves steal 600-diamond necklace from Vienna museum in broad daylight
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxvwpe0plro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Thieves steal 600-diamond necklace from Vienna museum in broad daylight - Published An international manhunt is under way for two men who stole a necklace decorated with more than 600 diamonds from a museum in Vienna after buying a ticket for the exhibition in which it was being displayed. Police said the two suspects smashed a glass display case at the Vienna Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) on Thursday afternoon and grabbed the platinum and diamond necklace, which is believed to be worth more than $4m (£3m; €3.5m). The necklace, which was designed for the former Egyptian royal family, was part of an exhibition on the jewellers Van Cleef & Arpels, due to run at MAK until September. The theft is the latest in a series of spectacular heists of artefacts at European museums. Vienna police released photos of the two suspects, who were unmasked, captured on security cameras. They are appealing for the public to come forward with information. The police said in a statement that one of the perpetrators was also believed to have been carrying what was thought to be a real firearm. After seizing the necklace, they fled "towards the Vienna Stadtpark" just south of the museum, they said. Lilli Hollein, MAK general director, said "the theft of a highly valuable piece of jewellery... has hit us hard". She said in a statement that MAK had developed a security plan with Van Cleef & Arpels specifically for the exhibition, adding: "Security issues were taken very seriously and all security measures were carefully prepared." Hollein said staff had reacted calmly and followed the established procedures when the "armed incident" occurred, and that no one had been injured. She added that MAK had thoroughly reviewed its security measures ahead of the exhibition, "particularly in light of the incidents at major museums in recent years". Also on Thursday was one of the most important troves of prehistoric jewellery and artefacts was stolen from a Spanish museum. Four Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily earlier this month, while three paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth millions of euros were taken from a museum in Parma earlier in the year. These heists came after the brazen daylight raid on the Louvre in Paris, in which a masked gang stole priceless jewels last October. The string of thefts have raised questions about the security of European cultural institutions. Europol said museum thefts were "becoming increasingly aggressive, with a shift towards violent and forceful methods", adding this "may indicate the involvement of new criminal networks". The necklace stolen in Vienna on Friday was designed for the former Egyptian royal family and was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter Fawzia to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. Van Cleef & Arpels describes it as a "triumph of white jewellery". The diamonds on the necklace weigh in excess of 200 carats. When it was auctioned a decade ago, it had an estimated worth of $3.6m-$4.6m. Police dog units have been deployed in Vienna and the province of Lower Austria, while forensic experts are analysing evidence and CCTV footage. The exhibition has now been reopened. - Published16 August - Published19 October 2025

item.title: Greenland says findings on genocide allegation not final
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxzv29p12lo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Greenland says findings on genocide allegation not final - Published Greenland's justice minister has said the government cannot conclude whether genocide was committed against the Inuit community after experts examined the use of forced contraception in the 1960s and 70s. "We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide," Marianne Paviasen told reporters. "This is something we can continue to debate." Two reports on the practice were released on Friday, a year after Denmark apologised for the treatment of Inuit women and girls in its autonomous territory. Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said a "reconciliation commission" would be set up while Danish PM Mette Frederiksen promised the governments would work together. Denmark has passed a compensation law to pay 300,000 Danish crowns (£34,404; $46,800) to each woman affected by the policy. Records from the national archives show that, between 1966 and 1970, 4,500 Greenlandic women and girls, some as young as 13, had an intra-uterine device (IUD) implanted under a birth-control programme administered by Danish doctors. In recent years, many women came forward to say they had been fitted with an IUD without their knowledge or consent. Use of the birth control was so widespread that Greenland's population growth severely slowed. Frederiksen issued an apology last August to Greenlandic women and their families affected by "systematic discrimination". In 2024, a former prime minister of Greenland, Mute B Egede, described the practice as "genocide". Under the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, external, one definition of genocide is "imposing measures intended to prevent births" within a "national, ethnical, racial or religious group". The territory tasked a panel of four experts with establishing whether human rights had been violated and whether such violations met the definition of genocide. However, the panel split, with two members resigning and producing a separate report. The two experts who remained, Alaskan lawyer Dalee Sambo Dorough and University of Copenhagen law professor Miriam Cullen, found in their report that the rights of Inuit women in Greenland had been violated. But they said that they could not conclude that genocide had taken place "on the basis of contraceptive practices alone". They added that genocidal intent by Denmark remained a "possible inference" that a court might establish, based on evidence that fell outside the scope of their report, such as the removal of Inuit children to be raised by Danish families. The rival report, produced by Jonas Christoffersen, former head of the Danish Institute for Human Rights, and Jensine Nedergaard, a psychologist who had worked in Greenland, accepted that women had been wronged but could not establish the extent of their mistreatment. They found no evidence "any authority or health professional at any time had any intention of destroying the Greenlandic population". Reacting on Friday, Greenland's justice minister said the two reports were so different that one "says there was no genocide at all" while the other "says there could have been". - Greenland contraception scandal victims hear Danish PM's emotional apology - Published24 September 2025 - Denmark apologises to Greenland's forced contraception victims - Published27 August 2025 - ‘Doctors fitted a contraceptive coil without my consent’ - Published8 December 2022 One woman affected by the forced contraception policy, Henriette Berthelsen, told news agency AFP before the reports were presented that their conclusions had been skewed from the start because no Greenlandic Inuits had been appointed as experts. "For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life and my right to self-determination," she said. "And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women." Another woman, Inger Platou, 70, told Reuters that she remembered waking up from what she had been told was a minor operation to discover an IUD had been inserted without her consent. "It turns out we were treated like animals," she said. "Without consent, they just wanted to stop women from giving birth or having children. It was a very inhumane act." A doctor, she added, later told her complications from the coil had left her unable to become pregnant. She went on to adopt two children from Colombia. "We are very deferential to authority because we are colonial children," she said. Reacting to the reports on Friday, Frederiksen said: "We will handle the political process together with the government of Greenland. The most important thing for me is that we find the right path together." Greenland was a Danish colony until 1953 and did not gain home rule until 1979. Copenhagen continued to oversee its healthcare system until 1992. The Inuit, or mixed Danish and Inuit, make up nearly 90% of the island's population of 56,000. The birth-control campaign was designed to control the territory's population, which had ballooned since the 1950s, aided by modernisation and better healthcare. This growth, in addition to an increasing rate of teenage pregnancies, had alarmed the Danish authorities. In 1970, the campaign was considered a "success" as fertility rates had fallen sharply, though the rate continued to fall for some time after that. In the eight years from the campaign's inception in 1966 until 1974 when it levelled off, Greenland's fertility rate plunged from seven children per woman to 2.3.

item.title: Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9zj11gwzxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues - Published A month after tens of thousands of migrants entered the city of Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa, there have been outbreaks of violence as tensions mount between locals and foreign arrivals. The Spanish government has been accused by opposition parties of struggling to manage the crisis effectively. Ceuta's residents have complained of feeling unsafe on the streets, as well as expressing concerns about the burden being placed on public services. At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor. The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most are sleeping rough on beaches or streets. Anti-migrant demonstrations earlier this month were largely peaceful, but in recent days they have become increasingly violent. On Thursday, several dozen locals prevented Red Cross personnel from distributing food and water to the migrants. Afterwards, some set fire to migrant camps on Trampolín beach, the main site where they have been sleeping, and there were also clashes with the police. Those incidents came hours after the arrest of 12 migrants who were accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, breaking its windows and injuring the four men inside. That same morning there were reports of vigilante groups pursuing migrants through the streets. Journalists and film crews have also reported being threatened. "This is a city which has been under pressure, […] which has the right to normality," the mayor of the exclave, the conservative Juan Jesús Vivas, told Antena 3 television. "The dignity of Spain is a stake right now in Ceuta," he said. The socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has appealed for calm and accused Vivas's People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox of stoking the tensions. José María Figaredo, a member of Congress for Vox, is being investigated for a possible hate crime after saying, soon after the migrants' arrival, that they should be "hunted down, one by one". Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told a congressional committee: "We have heard during these weeks rhetoric and comments that contribute to the stigmatisation of immigrants and which feed social division at a moment when what we need is responsibility and statesmanship." Javier Celaya, who represents Ceuta in Congress for the PP, accused the government of treating "the invaders as victims when the real victims are us, the people of Ceuta". On Friday, all the parties in the Ceuta local assembly signed a declaration condemning violence. Earlier this week, the government centralised management of the situation, overriding the local authority, after criticism that it had been slow to respond. Defence Minister Margarita Robles also apologised to those in Ceuta who "may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared", as the government unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws. Much of the recent ill-feeling in the city appears to be driven by government plans to move migrants into existing public buildings, such as sports centres, in order to be able to process their legal status in an orderly way and return those not eligible for asylum to Morocco. Many local people, and Vivas, oppose this initiative, due to concerns that it will move the migrants closer to residential areas. The government is also facing questions about who was behind the mass migrant crossing. Politicians on the right and the far left have accused Morocco of involvement, pointing to its alleged use of the border with Spain in the past to exert political pressure. Sánchez and his Socialist Party instead blame people traffickers, insisting that Rabat is a reliable partner which facilitated the immediate return of most of the arrivals. Nonetheless, the crisis has placed the sovereignty of Ceuta, and its fellow autonomous city Melilla, under the spotlight. Morocco has maintained a longstanding claim to the territories, which it has reiterated in recent weeks. Spain's Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he "roundly rejected" such comments by Morocco. "I don't speak about, nor have I spoken about, nor are we going to speak about Spain's territorial integrity with Morocco or with anyone else," he told the congressional committee. item.title: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0j38d9v40po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34 - Published A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minster announced. Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father. The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US. Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power. Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch, external, ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century. Announcing his death, Tooro's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki called his passing on Thursday an "immeasurable loss" to the royal family and the people of Tooro. "I call upon all the people of Tooro to remain united, calm and prayerful during this profoundly difficult time," Akiiki said on Friday. "May His Majesty the King rest in eternal peace." The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch. Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured". "His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained. When he became king in 1995 a regency, which included the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation. The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness. The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda. Similarly, the Rwenzururu Kingdom also extended its condolences to "all those mourning this great loss", according to local media reports. Others have also paid their respects to the late king. The Federation of Uganda Football Associations, honoured King Oyo as a "true friend of the beautiful game", and announced a moment of silence before the kick-off of all matches until 4 September in memory of his "legacy, love, passion and contribution" to the sport. Government minister Margaret Muhanga described the mood in the kingdom as "sombre... you can't see anyone smiling". The king was "at the prime of his life", she said in a video shared on social media, "as young as he was, he had an impact on his kingdom". Muhanga said they would be planting a million trees in his honour during the mourning period, and wants to ask the neighbouring districts in Tooro to do the same. Uganadan musician Juliana Kanyomozi called it a "very dark day for Tooro", in an Instagram post. "Gone too soon. What a loss!!!!" Meanwhile, pop star-turned-politician Bobi Wine, called for King Oyo's "soul to rest in eternal peace". 1 of 4 More BBC stories from Uganda - The 'shadow army' helping Uganda's long-serving president keep an iron grip on power - Published17 October 2025 Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. item.title: US plans to cut off military aid to key Middle East ally, BBC told
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn74m8e5rleo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US plans to cut off military aid to key Middle East ally, BBC told - Published The Trump administration is planning to cut off military aid to a key Middle East ally that helped the US defeat the Islamic State group (IS) and is now facing punishing attacks from Iran, according to four sources familiar with the matter. The US Department of Defense has told leaders of Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region in recent meetings that the administration is not planning to renew an expiring agreement that provides security assistance to the Peshmerga, the Kurdish security force. The BBC spoke to two officials who participated in the talks and two other sources with direct knowledge of the issue. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the talks, details of which have not been previously reported. Kurdish officials fear the funding cut would create a power vacuum and embolden Iran, which has fired hundreds of missiles and drones into Iraqi Kurdistan since US President Donald Trump started the war with Tehran. Ending the Peshmerga's security assistance would undermine a longtime partner in Iraq, analysts said, and send the message that the US cannot be trusted to back its allies in the region. "The US would be cutting off the Kurds, who shed so much blood to help the Americans achieve their goals in Iraq and the wider Middle East," Yerevan Saeed, the director of the Global Kurdish Initiative for Peace at American University, said. "This is going to be a big win for Iran, China, and Russia if the Kurds are left so exposed." In his second term, Trump has pledged to reduce America's foreign entanglements in regions like the Middle East. He also launched the war with Iran, which reached the six-month mark on Friday with no end in sight. The memorandum of understanding between the Pentagon and the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) is set to expire on 30 September, the same day the US and other nations are withdrawing their last remaining troops from Iraq. The troop withdrawal will formally end the international military campaign against IS, in which the Peshmerga fought alongside coalition troops to end the jihadist group's control of parts of Iraq and Syria. The sole remaining US military base in the country, located in the Iraqi Kurdish capital of Irbil, is set to close next month once coalition troops leave. The Peshmerga, which has approximately 180,000 troops in Iraqi Kurdistan, received $61m (£45m) in the fiscal year 2026 for weapons, military training and stipends through the Pentagon's counter-IS programme. The Pentagon proposed cutting all the group's security aid in its fiscal year 2027 budget request - arguing that since IS was defeated the money should now be reallocated - but the spending plan is on hold amid a broader budget battle in Congress. The request raised alarm bells in Iraqi Kurdistan, but officials had held out hope that the US would renew the funding through an extension of the current deal. The fears have only grown as Iran has stepped up attacks against the KRG. Iran and Iranian-backed militias had conducted 158 missile or drone attacks inside Iraqi Kurdistan by late May, according to reasearch on the latest available data compiled by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington DC think tank. But despite the surge in attacks, in recent talks with Iraqi and Kurdish leaders, defence department officials said the US was not planning to extend the memorandum of understanding, multiple sources with knowledge of the discussions said. The Pentagon signed the initial memorandum of understanding giving military assistance to the Peshmerga in 2016 and renewed it in 2022. A final decision on security engagement between the US and Kurdistan is still being reviewed, according to one source familiar with the Pentagon's thinking. The US is considering ways to maintain some security support in both Iraq and Iraqi Kurdistan after the troop withdrawal, the sources said. - Six months into the Iran war, what has Trump accomplished? - Published15 hours ago Both the KRG and US State Department declined to comment. In response to questions about security assistance for the Peshmerga, a Pentagon spokesperson referred to a statement by the department summarising Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's meeting with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in July. "The United States, Iraq and Coalition partners have achieved tremendous success in defeating ISIS and now the Iraqi Security Forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, will lead the fight against terrorists in Iraq," the statement said. The expiration of the security aid for the Peshmerga would come less than one year after the US opened its largest consulate in the world, in Irbil. At the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the $800m complex last December, Michael Rigas, a senior US State Department official, said the consulate was "a testament to the value of the relationship between the United States and the Iraqi Kurdistan Region". The recent discussions around Kurdish security were part of larger conversations between the US, the Iraqi government and KRG over the upcoming troop withdrawal. That date was set under a 2024 agreement between Washington and Baghdad to withdraw the US troops that remain in Iraq from the campaign against IS. American combat troops left Iraq in 2011 but returned after the power vacuum led to the rise of IS in 2014. The US could avoid repeating the same mistake by continuing to back the Peshmerga, said James Jeffrey, who spearheaded the global coalition against IS in Trump's first term. "It's money well spent, as we found out when the Islamic State rolled into northern Iraq," said Jeffrey, a former US ambassador to Iraq and Turkey under the Obama administration. The Trump administration has not said how many US troops brought in to fight IS more than a decade ago remain in Iraq. Experts believe it's under 1,000, down from 170,000 at the height of the Iraq War. The recent meetings on Iraqi security included the White House, Defense and State Departments, with Tom Barrack acting as a principal US voice on Iraq, four sources said. A close Trump ally, Barrack is the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Iraq and Syria. The administration has said publicly it's open to a bilateral security agreement with Iraq. The countries discussed a possible defence pact in the recent meetings, but it's still unclear how the agreement might be structured or what Iraqi Kurdistan's role might be. Al-Zaidi touted the troop withdrawal during his visit to Washington last month. Al-Zaidi, who was elected in May, met Trump at the White House, as well as Hegseth and members of Congress. "October 1 will mark a new day in the trajectory of the Iraqi state, as Iraq will be free of any foreign military presence," al-Zaidi's office said in a statement at the time. The withdrawal will reduce the exposure of US troops in the Middle East who have been targeted by Iran during the war, analysts said. Tehran has attacked US bases across the region, including the base in Irbil. But it will leave the Peshmerga security force and the rest of the region it helps protect even more vulnerable than before, said Jason Campbell, a former US defence official. "The Peshmerga have been the frontline in the US and international war with ISIS," said Campbell, an expert at the Middle East Institute. "If the US moves forward with this, it'll make the Kurds perhaps the most vulnerable potential targets of Iran." Related topics - Published5 March - Published13 March

item.title: Two-year curfew lifted in Sudan's capital
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2076gxr0llo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Two-year curfew lifted in Sudan's capital - Published Sudan's military-led government has lifted a curfew and state of emergency in Khartoum imposed more than two years ago, state media says. The authorities are taking this step 18 months after the army seized back control of the capital from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which it has been fighting in a civil war now in its fourth year. But clashes continue in the south and west, with mounting evidence that the war is spilling across Sudan's borders. More than two million of the roughly five million people who fled Khartoum after war erupted in April 2023 have returned to the city since fighting there ended in March 2025, according to the International Organization for Migration. The aim of lifting the curfew is to help restore normal life to the capital. The government has reopened the city's main airport for some flights and is encouraging businesses and embassies to come back. But residents still struggle to rebuild their livelihoods. Many have found widespread damage with many buildings looted. And they have to cope with constant power blackouts, due to alleged RSF drone attacks on electricity infrastructure and a lack of government funds to carry out repairs. "The targeting of the electricity sector in particular was very significant," a spokesperson for the Khartoum state government, Altayeb Saadeldin, told the Reuters news agency, listing looting of copper wires and fuel and other components, as well as drone attacks, as reasons for the outages. An RSF source responded that the allegations were "incorrect and army propaganda". - Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity - Published7 August Despite lifting the state of emergency, the authorities remain wary of RSF infiltration. The Sudan News Agency said security patrols would continue operating across the state and locals traveling at night would need to carry identification documents. Reports compiled by BBC Monitoring say the army continues to carry out security sweeps across greater Khartoum, targeting alleged RSF sleeper cells, undocumented foreigners and criminals involved in illegal activities. In the meantime, there is growing concern that the war is drawing in neighbouring countries. Chad is accusing the Sudanese army of carrying out an air strike that hit a military convoy in Ennedi-Est province, about 100km (62 miles) inside Chadian territory, on 20 August. It has reportedly put its forces along the border on maximum alert. Sudan has rejected the charge, saying it is surprised that its army was blamed without an independent investigation. In a statement, the foreign ministry said it "affirms that the Sudanese army fulfils its constitutional duty to defend Sudan's sovereignty, security and territorial integrity, and to confront the threats facing the country, while remaining committed to respecting the sovereignty of neighbouring states and refraining from targeting their territories". Sudan accuses Chad of permitting the passage of RSF military supplies delivered by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) through its airports and border crossings. The UAE and Chad deny the allegations despite similar findings by UN experts and investigative reports by international media. The attack on the Chadian convoy prompted the US Senior Adviser for Arab and African Affairs, Massad Boulos to express "deep concern" about the risk of Sudan's war threatening regional peace and stability. Boulos has been urging the parties to immediately accept a humanitarian truce. He has grown increasingly frustrated with the Sudanese military, which refuses to engage in a peace process unless the RSF disarms and withdraws from the territory it has occupied. "The United States condemns the SAF's recent air strikes inside Chad," Boulos wrote in a post on X. "There is no military solution to this conflict - and absolutely no justification for expanding the violence beyond Sudan's borders. "External financial and military support to the warring parties must stop," he added. This month the US envoy presented a draft resolution to the UN Security Council that would extend a 2005 weapons embargo on Darfur - the stronghold of the RSF - across the entire country and include a ban on attack drones, which are increasingly used by both sides. Sudan's government and army have rejected the proposal. According to local media reports officials argue that this unfairly equates the recognised national military with a paramilitary force and restricts its ability to defend citizens against an insurgency. item.title: Shootings surge as drug gangs torment Brussels
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9w4r7e7z4ko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Shootings surge as drug gangs torment Brussels - Published Last Monday night, drug gangs turned Salvatore's pizzeria in Brussels into a crime scene. "We dropped to the floor. I had clients eating on the terrace with children. Look, we can see the bullet impacts everywhere." His restaurant sits on a pretty little square in St Gilles. It's a central area of the city, close to the international Midi train station, where passengers arrive on trains from London and Paris. Shootings related to drug trafficking have become routine in the Belgian capital over the past couple of years. There were over 100 in 2025 alone, and more than 65 shootings so far this year. This was the third shooting in this neighbourhood in just three days. "Are we in an American gangster movie? This needs to stop," Salvatore says. A suspected drug dealer was shot in the leg in the same area the day before. Now Murielle and her dog Chéva are sitting at that exact spot, just across the street: "We can still see the trace of the pool of blood." Murielle is 70, and hopes peace soon returns to her street. "I like it here. It's like a little village inside the city. Even the drug dealers used to be polite and decent. I would just tell them to go further away and they'd say, 'Yes, ok mama!'" Drug dealing is happening in plain sight here. Only five minutes after I arrive, I witness a transaction. A buyer walks up to the seller, shakes their hand, and walks away with the drugs. Crack has become widely consumed amongst the poorest in this area of Brussels. "Things have changed in the past six months," says Murielle. "The business has intensified. Sometimes you even see consumers queuing to buy drugs. And now gangs are fighting over this spot." A successful drug-dealing point in Brussels nets up to €50,000 ($58,000; £43,000) per day or more for the dealer, according to the chief of Brussels South Police, Jurgen de Landsheer. Organised crime in the Belgian capital has become significantly more violent, he says. At the heart of it all is money. There are more than 200 drug-dealing points across the city, according to the police. The rise of drug-related violence in the Belgian capital echoes the situation of other European cities such as the French port of Marseille. Cocaine has become widely available in Europe, the continent's ports serving as entry points for the drug. The port of Antwerp, just 40km (25 miles) away, has seen record cocaine seizures in recent years. Jurgen de Landsheer says gangs in Brussels are now adopting methods seen in Marseille, although he insists his city has not reached the same level of violence. "We don't have no-go zones here in Brussels. It's not easy to go in some neighbourhoods, but we go everywhere. We don't want to become like some neighbourhoods in Marseille, so we'll do everything to stop it." A police station even came under attack last weekend. CCTV footage shows two men on a scooter stopping in front of the building and shooting at the door several times with what looks like an AK-47 before leaving on their scooter. This marks an escalation, as it is the first time criminals have targeted police. Usually, the shootings involve rival gangs. "We see a lot of young people getting paid a few hundred euros. They get a weapon, AK-47 or other heavy weapon, and then they get a mission. To shoot a person in the leg, for example, or to try to kill somebody. And they get very little money for this." De Landsheer says some of the people his men arrest are as young as 12, and that makes it very dangerous for the whole community. "The biggest danger is a stray bullet." There is no magic solution. We need prevention over repression The spike in shootings has forced Belgian authorities to react and, on Thursday, Belgium's interior minister announced that an extra 40 police officers would be deployed in the problem area. Jurgen de Landsheer is aware that police alone will not solve this crisis. "There is no magic solution. We need prevention over repression. We can do our part and be present in the street, but our society also needs to give a future to the young people, do something with them. That's the social part." Back in St Gilles, Salvatore says it's time for the violence to end. "Nobody sleeps here at the moment. People talk about moving out, houses are losing value." Murielle wants to believe that the worst is now behind. "We will not be intimidated. We'll carry on living and we'll keep on protecting our lovely neighbourhood."

item.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgwdn1g58yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America - Published US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America. The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs next month. Trump said the renaming of the lake, which straddles both countries, was effective immediately. He has broad discretion over how the US recognises landmarks but other countries do not have to follow. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in response that "things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever". The executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US. Carney noted that the name Lake Ontario could be traced back more than 400 years, adding that it preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence. "We know that the United States is changing," he said. "Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms. "Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever." There is no universally recognised international body setting the names of international waters. When Trump took to the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water. It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application., external In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)". The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing. Canadian officials dismissed Trump's move to rename the lake. Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote: "It's Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever." Other premiers and ministers made similar statements. The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York. There was a mixed reaction from US politicians. Trump's Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum applauded the move, writing: "We're on it, Mr. President!" "The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States," he said, adding that the US Geological Survey "maps our country for the world to see, and we are PROUD to implement your Executive Order to rename LAKE AMERICA". But Democratic lawmaker Debbie Dingell of Michigan, the US state that borders four of the five Great Lakes, said that she would introduce a bill in Congress to nullify the name change, calling Trump's order "idiotic". She wrote: "The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect". Democratic New York Governor Kathy Hochul said her state, the sole US state bordering Lake Ontario, would not be calling it Lake America. As he signed the order on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said it was not a direct message to Canada, but that America's northern neighbour "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade". US-Canada relations have fallen to a new low, with insults thrown back and forth over the past week. But there was a hint on Thursday that there was room for a return to the negotiating table. Canadian US trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said the US had withdrawn some of its demands around labelling requirements in French, one of the sticking points. The US has maintained it never made demands about language. Both sides have accused the other of demanding last-minute changes that caused the breakdown in trade negotiations. item.title: Dutch court sentences man to life over Rwanda genocide
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce8x96rw79ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Dutch court sentences man to life over Rwanda genocide - Published A court in the Netherlands has sentenced a Dutch-Rwandan man to life for his involvement in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. The 66-year-old, named only as Eugene N, was accused, among other things, of throwing a hand grenade into a crowd of Tutsis who were seeking shelter in a stadium. He was convicted of war crimes and the crime of genocide, having acted with "genocidal intent", the judge said. Rwanda had sought his extradition in 2014 but the authorities in the Netherlands then launched their own investigation into N, who had become a Dutch citizen. In 100 days in April 1994, an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus people were killed by Hutu extremists. The court in The Hague heard N held an authoritative position in the community at the time of the massacre, overseeing around 1,000 people in Mbazi in southern Rwanda. "The suspect was a man who was held in high regard and must have been aware of his role and the influence he had as a local administrator," the court explained, adding that he "committed multiple severe crimes". At a football stadium, he instructed Hutus not to let any of the Tutsis escape. Trapped inside, they were pelted with stones, shot at and had hand grenades thrown at them. Any who had survived, were killed with clubs and machetes, the court said. Prior to the stadium massacre, N had watched on as people looted houses and set them on fire. "Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families," the court said. As part of the Dutch investigation opened in 2020, more than 30 witnesses were interviewed. N was subsequently arrested in 2024. N denied all the charges, the AFP news agency reports, alleging that he was a victim who had lost family in "those horrific events". "The case has torn his scars open again. He is a broken man," his lawyers are quoted as saying by AFP. They had moved to seek acquittals on all accounts. N was acquitted of the incitement to genocide. His defence team said they will "almost certainly appeal the charges", according to local news agency ANP. - Rwanda's 100 days of slaughter - Published4 April 2019 - My return home - 30 years after Rwanda's genocide - Published6 April 2024 - 'I forgave my husband's killer - our children married' - Published24 April 2022 Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. item.title: Tate brothers blast US jail conditions as they seek bail in UK extradition fight
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9v9nndjznvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Tate brothers blast US jail conditions as they seek bail in UK extradition fight - Published Andrew and Tristan Tate have told a Florida court they should be released from jail so they can fight extradition to the UK on charges of rape and trafficking. Wearing tan jail uniforms, the brothers maintained they did not commit the alleged crimes as they hit out at conditions in US custody. Government lawyers argued the two were a flight risk and had bragged about having multiple passports, while defence attorneys said the social media influencers' high profile would make it almost impossible for them to flee. US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis will issue a written ruling at a later date on whether to grant bail to the dual British-US citizens. The pair were arrested in Miami on 19 July. During Thursday's hearing, defence lawyers said the brothers had complied with the terms of their release while they battled the UK charges and another case in Romania. US authorities took the men into custody last month after the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) unveiled dozens of new charges against them. The British authorities have until 16 September to submit a full extradition request. - Will the Tate brothers be extradited from the US to the UK? - Published21 July The brothers, who arrived in court in shackles, were questioned in turn by their defence attorneys and government lawyers as they took the stand. Andrew Tate, 39, declared he has "never committed the crimes I'm accused of". Tristan Tate, 38, described his detention conditions as small and hot, with little sunlight and exercise. "It's beginning to grate on me because I can't partake in helping with my defence," he told the court, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. "It's death by scurvy," he said, adding that he had lost 14lb (6.3kg). The British Embassy filed court documents asking the judge to keep the Tates in custody as the UK pursues extradition. US government lawyers pushed back against the brothers' claims that they had exaggerated their wealth to massage their online personas. The federal attorneys said the Tates had access to resources that could help fund an escape and they had bragged about having multiple passports. But Andrew Tate, a former professional kickboxer, testified that to support himself financially, he "had to go back to the boxing ring against heavier, younger opponents", according to CBS News. "I've said some stupid things, but sometimes you have to shake the internet to get noticed," he testified about his online statements, according to CBS. "This is the reality of the internet. "I'm being treated like El Chapo," he added, referring to the Mexican drug kingpin, "but I have a perfect record in the court system". Under questioning from his attorney, Joseph McBride, Andrew Tate denied he was a human trafficker. The defence also called Natasha Sesay, from England, to testify in support of releasing Andrew Tate. She described a five-year romantic relationship, saying she had had one child with him and was expecting a second. "It's nice having him at home," she told the court, reports CBS. Sesay also said that despite his online persona, Andrew Tate "has never ever been violent toward women", according to CBS. The UK has brought a total of 59 criminal charges against the Tates, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child. The British authorities filed 21 charges last year against the brothers, then 38 additional counts last month. The combined charges involve seven accusers, UK prosecutors said. The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025. "If I go to England they will lock me up," Tristan Tate said on the stand in Miami on Thursday, "and take everything I've ever worked for". He also said the Romanian charges had "destroyed my entire life", reports CBS. "They took everything, even the savings accounts for their [his children's] college funds. This case is make or break for me." The Tates built an influencer empire in the so-called manosphere, showcasing a lifestyle of conspicuous wealth and excess. Andrew Tate accumulated millions of followers among an audience of primarily young men. The White House has said President Donald Trump will not intervene in the extradition case of the brothers, who have been vocal supporters of him.
