item.title: Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2q7z5mlrmo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules - Published A judge has ruled the US Department of Defense acted unlawfully when it designated artificial intelligence (AI) startup Anthropic a supply chain risk, calling the move "illegal and baseless". The company argued in the lawsuit that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth overstepped his authority with the new designation. It followed Anthropic's refusal to allow the military to use its AI models for tasks including surveillance or autonomous weapons. US District Judge Rita Lin said in the ruling that citing national security was "not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics". Anthropic welcomed the ruling. The BBC has contacted the Pentagon and the White House for comment. Anthropic was focused on "working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology", a spokesperson told the BBC. Judge Lin said in the court filing that the Defense Department had acted unlawfully to order firms that do business with the US military to boycott Anthropic. The Pentagon designated Anthropic as a supply-chain risk in February - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US. It marked the first time an American company had been publicly designated as such. Anthropic's lawsuit said the government's actions were both "unprecedented and unlawful". The Claude maker said its models were not reliable enough to be safely used in weapons systems for the military. It added that it opposed its use for domestic surveillance as a violation of rights. The Pentagon said at the time that private companies should not be able to constrain military action. The White House had previously said Anthropic was "a radical left, woke company attempting to control military activity" and argued the military was beholden to the US Constitution, "not any woke AI company's terms of service". The Pentagon also argued that Anthropic's refusal to accept new contract terms raised concerns over what the company could do with its technology. Anthropic said in its lawsuit that its business had been impacted by the government's actions and its right to freedom of speech had been violated. Judge Lin said during an earlier round in the lawsuit that the government was trying to "cripple" the company and "chill public debate" over military use of AI. "This appears to be classic First Amendment retaliation," the judge added. - Published1 day ago - Published9 June

item.title: Fed has 'work to do' if price rises don't ease for Americans, Warsh says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9zjgv9lgdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Fed has 'work to do' if price rises don't ease for Americans, Warsh says - Published The head of the US central bank has said policymakers will "have work to do" if they were not confident cost-of-living pressures were easing for Americans. Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said while inflation readings looked better than expected over the summer, they did not show that the current picture had "meaningfully improved". The new Fed boss stressed that his remarks should not be treated as a guide for future interest rate decisions, but the comments are a signal rates could be raised if policymakers believe inflation is too high. Latest figures show prices rose 3.4% in the year to July, above the Fed's 2% target. Another inflation measure closely watched by the Fed is running at 3.7%. Warsh made the comments in his first speech at the annual Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in Wyoming, which sees central bankers, government officials and academics from around the world gather to talk about interest rates, inflation and other economic issues. Warsh said given prices were rising by more than 2% on annual basis, "the Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices". "Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do." The central bank boss has remained tight-lipped about the potential path of interest rates, but investors will have watched his speech closely for any signs of the Fed's approach under his leadership. The central bank's next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September. The reactions to any decision made by US President Donald Trump will be closely watched, with the mid-term elections looming and voters concerned about affordability. Trump, who appointed Warsh in May, repeatedly criticised and pushed his predecessor Jerome Powell to cut interest rates. The president has previously said rate hikes "just keeps the country down". Warsh issued a plea in his speech to not label his remark as "forward guidance" and said he believed the practice of sending signals to the markets on future interest rate decisions, adopted in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, had "overstayed its welcome". "Oversharing policy deliberations and overcommitting to future decisions can lead markets, businesses, and households astray," he said, adding it also inhibited the Fed the "freedom to make the right calls when it's time to decide". Interest rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row amid concerns over inflation due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices. Following Warsh's remarks, the rates market showed growing expectations of an interest rate rise in September, according to CME data. Analysts at Capital Economics said Warsh's speech delivered a "far clearer - and hawkish - message" and that it left "the door open to a hike" earlier than previously expected. "Hikes are not guaranteed, but Warsh is now at least suggesting he is on board with them if economic growth remains strong and monthly core PCE [Personal Consumption Expenditures] price growth remains a bit too firm," they said. - Why the US economy is ringing alarm bells - Published7 days ago Higher oil prices has also fuelled bond market investors, who have demanded higher returns, leading to higher borrowing costs for the US government and other major corporations. Such borrowing costs impact the cost of borrowing for mortgages, car loans and credit cards. The spike in interest payments has driven US national debt past the $40tn (£29.5tn). The figure has doubled in a decade under both the Trump and Joe Biden administrations. The figure is rising by about $90,000 (£66,500) every second, or $7.8bn a day, according to the Congress Joint Economic Committee. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the government would buy back more debt in a bid to lower borrowing costs, but the market's reaction to the announcement proved short lived. Interest rate hikes are a tool used by central banks aiming to slow the pace prices are rising in the shops. By pushing up the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, central bankers hope consumers will spend less and the rate of price increases will slow. Higher interest rates, however, can lead to better returns for savers.

item.title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd68vpjv21do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages - Published New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse. Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations. More than 550 people have been killed, Nepalese officials say, with hundreds more missing. Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera. The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape. Damage and mud can be seen more than 2.5km (1.5 miles) upstream, reaching 100m (330 ft) above the area it first hit. A few miles further south is the village of Timure, which has now largely disappeared. The walls of the valley at this point are steep, reaching up to 50m above the water line. The image shows most of the houses perched on this slope are now gone or covered in mud. A further 10km (eight miles) downstream, where the Trishuli River winds through Syapru Besi, satellite imagery now shows the village covered by mud, rock and other debris. Houses and other structures have disappeared, including bridges and a hydroelectric power station. One of the larger villages to be struck by the full force of the flood was Trishuli, where some of the earliest verified footage of the disaster emerged from. A satellite image of the town and surrounding agricultural land, which is about 45km (28 miles) downstream from the border, show an entire neighbourhood has been essentially washed away. Verified videos of the town show a bridge collapsing as the river surges forward. At the very same moment from ground level, footage filmed from inside a bus shows people crying out in distress and trying to flee as they see the water rushing down the river. Other dramatic videos show people sheltering inside a house, peering over the edge of a balcony as they watch a torrent of floodwater wash away almost everything around them, knocking large metal debris and a vehicle toward the building. Somehow the house remains intact and survivors can be seen in a second verified video standing surrounded by mud once the floodwater had receded. Imagery from satellite provider Planet Labs released today has also provided a clearer view of the disaster's origins at the collapsed glacier, the moment of which has been captured on a verified drone video. The satellite image shows an enormous chunk of the glacier has fallen away, carving an enormous path of rock and debris where water rushed through the valley. At the base of the landslide, trees and other vegetation have been stripped at a height of more than 300m above the riverbed. This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards. Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts. Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly. But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake. Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised. The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area. The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead. Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Mike Hill. - Published10 hours ago - Published3 hours ago - Published1 hour ago

item.title: Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clykn5p5172o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises - Published Norway's King Harald V has died at the age of 89, after he was taken to hospital last week for treatment for a rare blood condition. The palace in Oslo said he passed away peacefully at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) on Friday at the national hospital in Oslo. The royal flag on the roof of the palace has been lowered to half-mast and a period of national mourning has been declared leading up to the day of his funeral. Crowds of mourners have streamed to the royal palace to lay flowers and flags. Harald was the nation's first king born there since the 14th Century. He has been succeeded by his son Haakon, 53, who will hold an extraordinary council of state with the government later on Friday. King Charles III sent his "most heartfelt condolences" at the death of his "dear cousin" - who was a second cousin to Queen Elizabeth II - while King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden remembered "a good friend to me, my family and to Sweden", wishing his godson Haakon "success and good fortune". After 35 years on the throne, Harald will be remembered as a popular and reforming figure who modernised the monarchy, broke with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure at Norway's most difficult moments. Royal observers say he was down-to-earth, respected and beloved, describing him as a "grandfather" of the nation and the "People's king" - a title also used by his father King Olav V. During his reign, the Norwegian monarchy became more egalitarian and transparent about the royal family's finances and health matters, Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen, historian and TV2 royal correspondent, told the BBC. Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, described the late king as "one of us", while Caroline Vagle, royal expert for Se og Hør magazine, said he had "always been very close to the people". "He has never been afraid to show emotion, humour or vulnerability, and that has made him very human." In the wake of the 2011 bomb and gun attacks on Oslo and the island of Utøya, Harald appealed to Norwegians to support each other and not "let fear take over". More recently, Harald and his family faced health challenges and scandal, especially over his daughter-in-law Mette-Marit's association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and her son Marius Borg Høiby's conviction for rape. He is survived by his wife of almost 58 years, Queen Sonja, their daughter Princess Märtha Louise, their son, the new King Haakon, and six grandchildren. Harald was born on 21 February 1937 on the Skaugum estate near Oslo. He was three when dictator Adolf Hitler ordered the Nazi German invasion of Norway early in World War Two. Harald's mother fled with her children across the border to Sweden, and they travelled to the US on the invitation of President Franklin D Roosevelt. Prince Harald returned with his family to Norway at the end of the war and completed his school and compulsory military service. He became crown prince in 1957, studying social science, history and economics at Balliol College in Oxford from 1960 to 1962. He met Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a businessman, at a party, but the crown prince had to wait nine years before he was allowed to marry her. Eventually he told his father that if he could not marry Sonja, he would stay single, King Harald once told Norway's public broadcaster, external. His father finally gave his consent and the couple wed in Oslo Cathedral on 29 August 1968. Harald's choice paved the way for his own two children to marry commoners too, and for Vagle, that "helped bring an end to a very male-dominated royal family". When his father became ill in 1990, the then-crown prince became regent. Harald then ascended to the throne when Olav died on 17 January 1991. The new king came into his own around 2000, according to historian Trond Norén Isaksen, growing from a shy man into someone much more open and empathetic. In July 2011, Harald faced his greatest challenge yet as king, when neo-Nazi Anders Breivik murdered eight people with a car bomb in Oslo before moving onto a youth camp on the island of Utøya, where he shot dead 69 others, most of them teenagers. He gave a televised address the next day, and weeks later he delivered a speech, empathising with the victims and their families as a father, grandfather, husband and king. On the verge of tears, his voice quivered and broke. "I can only imagine the depth of your pain. As king of this nation, I feel for each and every one of you," he said. Looking back, historian Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen said: "I think that moment has been burned into our minds of what a monarchy should be." In 2016, the king made headlines again by giving a, external speech, external supporting diversity of religion, ethnicity and sexual orientation. He said Norwegians were from "Afghanistan, Pakistan and Poland, from Sweden, Somalia and Syria", that they "believe in God, Allah, the Universe and nothing", and that they "are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other". The king was also a keen athlete and environmentalist - one of the initiators of the Norwegian branch of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), who served as president of the Norwegian chapter for 20 years. He was such an accomplished sailor, he represented Norway three times at the Olympics. When Crown Prince Haakon married Mette-Marit in 2001, the king and queen welcomed her four-year-old son from a previous relationship. Høiby was treated as one of the family, but the royal house later stressed that he was never a royal. The king's daughter Princess Märtha Louise initially married a Norwegian writer before controversially remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024. The couple's business activities eventually led to her halting her royal duties. While some Norwegians may have felt Harald was too lenient with his family's controversial life decisions, Vagle believes he had "shown himself to be someone who puts talking things through ahead of issuing harsh instructions". As the king's health declined, he permanently reduced his public engagements in April 2024. More recently, he was treated with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia, which causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced. He entered hospital on 17 August and his son became regent, assuming his activities. This year alone the Norwegian royal family has faced compounded personal health challenges and scandals. The rape trial of Høiby, convicted of multiple offences in June, hung over the royal family for many months. He has now appealed against a four-year jail term and appeared at Harald's bedside shortly before he died. Days before the trial began, documents were released revealing his mother Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. She later apologised to Harald and Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement". Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant. She had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis eight years prior. Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and King Haakon will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her. The crises surrounding the monarchy have had an effect on its popularity. One poll for newspaper Aftenposten found that support had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%. Other polls suggested almost half of Norwegians believed Mette-Marit could no longer become queen, although Haakon is now highly likely to say she will. However, Vagle said criticism was rarely directed at the late king personally, leaving her with the impression that "everyone has loved King Harald". "When things go wrong in the royal family, people tend to blame anyone but the king," Isaksen remarked. Haakon has faced questions about the turbulence surrounding his own household that will "follow him into his position as a king", according to Taalesen, however she believes he has shown leadership and dealt with recent events well. The royal family's main strategy has been to separate itself from Høiby's trial, and Schulsrud-Hansen believes that has largely succeeded. Although there may be further scrutiny over the Epstein files, the focus for Norwegians now will be on remembering a "greatly beloved king" and supporting his son.

item.title: King Haakon begins reign after turbulent year for Norwegian monarchy
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp841114eg6o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Who is Norway's new King Haakon VIII? - Published King Haakon VIII has inherited the Norwegian throne after the death of his father, Harald V. Many in Norway believe he has big shoes to fill. King Harald was immensely popular with ordinary Norwegians, as shown by his consistent high polling and the outpouring of emotion in the lead-up to his death. Haakon is the fourth king to head Norway's modern monarchy, since it was restored in 1905 after the country gained independence from Sweden. Among his first duties as monarch, he led an extraordinary cabinet meeting where he announced his royal title and adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway". Many commentators believe he is well-placed to follow in his predecessors' footsteps. As crown prince, Haakon worked closely with his father as he carried out his royal duties and in recent years was handed more responsibility, increasingly acting as regent while Harald was ill or absent. "I am so lucky that Crown Prince Haakon is the one who will carry this forward," King Harald wrote of his son in his biography The King Tells. Historian Trond Norén Isaksen tells the BBC that Haakon will be a different type of king to his father, but no less respected. "King Harald... [was] very charismatic, he [had] a great sense of humour, which everyone appreciates, and Haakon is a bit more reserved, a bit more like his mother. "But in recent years he has also become a bit more relaxed and opened up a bit and showed a bit more of his sense of humour... he has been pulling enormous weight for many years given his parents have become older and his wife has been ill." Haakon is a great-great-great-grandson of Britain's Queen Victoria. His daughter Ingrid Alexandra, 22, now becomes the crown princess and heir to the Norwegian throne. Haakon was ahead of his older sister, Princess Märtha Louise, in the line of succession. The constitution was changed in 1990 to give women the right to inherit the throne, so Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra is in line to be Norway's first female head of state since the 15th Century. Haakon has become the king at a turbulent time for Norway's royal family. The monarchy remains broadly popular among Norwegians and has been long praised for its modern outlook. But in recent years it has been beset by scandal. Only this year, Haakon's wife Mette-Marit, now Queen of Norway, has apologised for several years of ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and her son has been convicted of rape in a high-profile trial. Marius Borg Høiby, who was born from an earlier relationship, is appealing against the conviction. Born in 1973, King Haakon is the youngest child of the late king and Queen Sonja. By Haakon's own admission, he struggled at times to accept his royal status in his early years. "Yes, I was a royal, but I did not want to talk about it... At school it made me anxious," he wrote in his 2023 autobiography, recalling his days in a state primary school in the 1980s. He became crown prince in 1991 at the tender age of 17, following the death of his grandfather King Olav V. Unusually for a royal, he was educated at local state schools before embarking upon a four-year-long naval career, graduating from the Norwegian Naval Academy in 1995. He decided not to follow his father and grandfather to Oxford University, instead flying to California to enrol at the University of Berkeley, where he studied political science. Soon after his return to Norway, Haakon met his now-wife Mette-Marit at a music festival in her home city of Kristiansand in 1999. She was dubbed by the press as the Cinderella of Kristiansand - a reference to her humble beginnings. "What we two found together was so strong that I could not let it go," the then-Crown Prince Haakon said of Mette-Marit ahead of their wedding in 2001. But their relationship was not without controversy and there was a fierce public debate in Norway from the moment Haakon first announced they were dating. Some commentators even warned at the time that their relationship could spell the end of the Norwegian monarchy, with comparisons being made to the infamous union between American divorcee Wallis Simpson and British King Edward VIII which led to his abdication in 1936. Queen Mette-Marit was not the first commoner to marry into the Norwegian royal family - the late King Harald had already broken with tradition by marrying Queen Sonja three decades earlier. She was, however, a single mother to a four-year-old child whose father had served time for a conviction of cocaine possession. The royal couple's co-habitation in an Oslo flat had also drawn criticism from the conservative Lutheran Church of Norway - though polls from the time showed most ordinary Norwegians did not care about either. What many Norwegians did question, though, was whether her former party lifestyle was one compatible with that of someone married to the future king. In an emotional interview three days before their marriage, Mette-Marit publicly apologised for her "wild past" and condemned drug use after reports that drugs were taken at parties she attended in Oslo during the 1990s. She did not say whether she had taken them herself. It was seen as something of a turning point. She won the affection of ordinary Norwegians and for years has been seen as the embodiment of a modern monarchy capable of shaking up convention. The couple have two children together, Ingrid and Prince Sverre Magnus. In her new role as crown princess, she took up popular causes including support for people with HIV and promoting literacy. Her diagnosis with pulmonary fibrosis in 2018 also led to widespread public sympathy. Haakon has said Mette-Marit helped him come out of his shell and described her as an emotional counterweight to his analytical mind. "I am not very good socially," he wrote. "Mette is a natural talent. She can go into a room and get along with everyone." But in recent times, Haakon's family has come under increasingly heavy public scrutiny and criticism. Marius Borg Høiby's rape conviction hangs over the family. One of women was raped on Haakon's estate at Skaugum outside Oslo. Høiby has always been treated as one of the family, although the royal house has repeatedly stressed he is not a royal. Days before his trial began, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later apologised to King Harald and Queen Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him. Several polls conducted earlier this year found nearly half of Norway's population felt the crown princess could not become queen, even though it was always bound to happen. Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant, eight years after her initial diagnosis. Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and the new king will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her. Caroline Vagle, royal correspondent for Se og Hør magazine, says in regards to Epstein the most important thing the royal family can do is be "completely open about what actually happened, and not allow public speculation to take on a life of its own". "But I also don't think we should overestimate the impact of one or two difficult cases," she says. "What will ultimately matter is how the royal family handles them, and how Haakon and the next generation manage to build on the trust that Harald has earned over a lifetime." Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, believes the scandals will be challenging but Haakon is "very much ready for the task". "I'm sure that in the future he will be respected and loved, similar to King Haakon VII, King Olav V and also King Harald V." Haakon's reign begins in the backdrop of these scandals, and how he navigates them might come to define his monarchy. - Published12 hours ago

item.title: 'Not far enough' - US parents and teens on Meta's new limits for young users
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2zn9zj361o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'Not far enough' - US parents and teens on Meta's new limits for young users - Published For Elizabeth Cardner, a mother of two girls in Houston, Texas, Meta's new limits on how teenagers can use its platforms are a welcome sign that more people are aware of social media's potential dangers. But, she tells the BBC, they probably won't help much in the long-term. "It will save a few arguments at home, but it doesn't go far enough," she says. This week, Meta announced new restrictions on its platforms - which include Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - as part of an $18bn (£13.25bn) settlement with US states in a lawsuit on social media's effects on children. The company said it would set a daily two-hour time limit, hide the number of likes that a post receives, remove autoplay on videos, mute push notifications during school hours, and ban extreme make-up filters. It also announced changes to its age-verification process and parental controls as well as agreeing to appoint an independent auditor to check the measures are implemented and maintained. Many parents across the US see the restrictions as helpful, but are still sceptical. Those who spoke to the BBC described feeling stuck - where they feel they can't cut their children off from social media but also can't protect them from the harms they believe it causes - and they are waiting to see how much of a difference these new rules will make. Cardner's 14-year-old, Paige, believes the restrictions will lead to "more real-life scenarios" and less "fake content", which she says dominates social media. She and her sister both approve of hiding the numbers of likes and restricting filters. But Paige sees those gains as short-lived, "since AI is evolving". "People will find new ways to have fake filters, and correct certain parts of their videos or pictures," she says. "So I think it'll help until people use other resources to try and find new ways to do that." Cardner says banning her daughters entirely from social media would only result in them being left out by their peers. "Damned if you do, damned if you don't," she says. "I don't think there's any winning on it." Another mother of two teens, Andria Rose, told the BBC that she feels defenceless and "no matter how much I protect my kids, Facebook, Instagram - they're coming in and literally, like, taking them out of their rooms". Even though she calls Meta's changes "fantastic", Rose, who lives near Boston, Massachusetts, doesn't believe they are fully addressing the problem. "They're trying to limit the drug, but they're not controlling the drug," she says. "They're still dealing." Rose notes her personal use of social media costs her sleep at night. "I'm hooked," she says. "So what do you think is going to happen to a kid?" The settlement was announced on Wednesday in the middle of a highly-anticipated trial, where Meta owner Mark Zuckerberg was expected to testify. The settlement did not include any admission of fault. The lawsuit was originally filed in 2023 by 29 US states, alleging Meta deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive and lied about risks. They also accused it of violating a federal law on collecting children's personal information. The settlement - announced this week - included 48 states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Several studies have found social media to be harmful to mental health, especially for children. Last year, a BBC investigation found children were being exposed to content about bullying, suicide and weapons on social media platforms. For Rose, Meta's settlement payment "is like throwing a couple of dollar bills at a problem", given how much money the company makes and how much she believes the industry profited from children during the pandemic. Joanie Story, a mother of four boys in Long Island, takes issue with another part of Meta's announcement - its conditions involving other platforms. The company will withhold $5bn of the settlement, and only release it if YouTube, TikTok and others also enter into similar agreements. It also said it would further tighten its time limit to one hour if other platforms implement similar restrictions. Story sees that as "petty". "That's like saying: 'You know, we have the ability to fix what is broken, but we're only gonna fix it halfway,'" she says. Still, Story is greeting the new rules as "good controls". She says she saw what a lack of controls could do when two of her sons were accidentally exposed to explicit content on a non-Meta platform. One boy has been in therapy for four years, she says. "It's almost like being abused," says Story. Mark SooHoo, a father of three who lives in the suburbs of Chicago, says social media and smartphones go hand-in-hand, and that both are harmful to young people. He belongs to Wait Until 8th, an organisation where parents pledge to not give their kids smartphones until the end of eighth grade, when most have finished middle school and are 13 or 14 years old. Most parents want to give their children smartphones so they aren't left out, he says. "And our message is very clear: We do want them to be left out. We want them to be left out of all the negative impacts of social media," SooHoo says. Instead of looking to the companies to address potential harms, SooHoo believes more parents should sign the smartphone pledge. item.title: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c70d41g40njo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped - Published Early on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife. She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Then the messages stopped. Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years. The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Thousands of Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years. Subhrasree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, she was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit. But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message. "After 08:03am, what happened? We don't know anything," he says. Subhrasree had been looking forward to the journey for years. The photographs she sent home from Kathmandu, taken just days before she went missing, capture something of that excitement. In one, she stands in a blue tunic in the ornate courtyard of a temple, smiling gently at the camera. In others, she is dressed in red, posing by the ancient brick-and-carved-wood architecture of Kathmandu valley's historic Durbar Square. She told her husband the countryside was beautiful. "She was very excited," says Bhattacharya, a government officer. "This was her dream tour." The journey had begun on Friday 21 August. She took the Mithila Express from Kolkata and reached Raxaul on 22 August. From there she crossed into Birgunj and travelled by bus to Kathmandu, arriving that night. She stayed in Kathmandu for three nights, sightseeing. Then, on the morning of 25 August, the group left Kathmandu by bus for Syabrubesi, a small mountain settlement roughly 122km north of Kathmandu and a gateway to the trekking hub of Langtang region. The journey took almost 12 hours - and was not entirely a smooth one. A landslide blocked their route for about four hours before the army cleared the road. But when Subhrasree spoke to her husband, she told him the skies were clear. There was little to suggest what was coming. "She kept saying the weather was good," he says. "She said it was rather warm, it was raining sometimes." The next morning, 26 August, Subhrasree left her hotel shortly after 07:00. Bhattacharya spoke to her on the phone, and the two continued messaging afterwards. Around an hour later, she told him the Nepal immigration formalities were complete and that the group was waiting to cross into Tibet. After clearing Nepal immigration, pilgrims cross the border on foot to the Chinese immigration facility in Gyirong. Bhattacharya believes his wife may have been inside, or close to, the Chinese immigration building when the disaster struck. "I knew there would be connectivity issues on the Tibet side," he says. "So I waited for the next message." At about 15:00, he saw reports of the floods in the media. He started calling pilgrims in her group. Nobody answered. He tried the tour operator and then the two managers accompanying the group. Again, there was no answer. The family has heard nothing from Subhrasree since. "Have they been rescued? Was this group among those rescued in China?" Bhattacharya asks. "We want to know more." He believes his wife and the others may already have crossed into Chinese territory before the floods struck. But he has received no confirmation of who made it across - or what happened to them afterwards. "Please get me a list from the Chinese government," he says. "Missing, dead and rescued. We need an update." Then comes the admission that captures the agony of those waiting at home: "What do I tell you? Sleepless nights, working on the phone." For the family of 54-year-old Rina Banerjee, there is more uncertainty. They do not even know which side of the border she was on when they lost contact. Rina, an unmarried private tutor from Kolkata, was travelling alone with a tour operator as part of the same pilgrimage group. Until then, her journey had appeared to be going smoothly. Her nephew, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, says the family had spoken to her over video calls while she was in Kathmandu. "She was happy," he says. "She was doing a trip after a long time." Rina was no stranger to mountains. She had travelled in the hills before and gone hiking with her family. "She was quite fit," Mukherjee says. "We have gone hiking. We are used to going to the mountains." She had told him about the landslide they encountered on the way the previous day. The group was stuck for about four hours, she had said. The next morning, the tour operator sent a group photograph, which showed Rina outside the Nepal immigration centre. Like Subhrasree, she had received her departure stamp, Mukherjee says. After that, silence. "I don't know whether they crossed the border or not," Mukherjee says. "Whether they were on the Chinese side or the Nepal side, we are still wondering." For Subhrasree, the two-week tour was to be her first pilgrimage, and a dream she had nurtured for years. Rina, too, had long wanted to make the journey and was no stranger to the mountains. Both women shared what Bhattacharya calls a "wanderlust" - a love of travelling, discovering new places and, in their case, heading into the mountains. Both had joined a group for the pilgrimage of a lifetime. Both appear to have cleared Nepal immigration, and both were believed to have crossed the border. Their names now appear on the Nepal government's official list , externalof 537 missing people. But that offers little clarity - their families still have no idea where they are or whether they are safe. The Kolkata-based tour operator says they have no information about the fate of the group yet. For both families, the journey has ended with the same unanswered question: did the women make it across the border?

item.description:

========================================
'The flood took everything': Nepal survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away - Published Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud. At least 469 people have died and several hundred others are missing after floods wiped out entire villages on the border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, with a force so powerful seismologists initially identified it as an earthquake. Rescuers trudged through thick mud and debris on Thursday as Nepalese authorities rushed to bring aid and relief supplies to the affected areas. "My family members were swept away by the flood in front of my eyes," Kalpana Malla from Nepal's Nuwakot district told the BBC. Malla said her father, mother, sister and sister's children were all claimed by the disaster. "They could not escape the flood; there was no chance at all," she said. "This flood took everything, but my son and I climbed the rooftop of a house and survived but couldn't explain how." Her son, Sugam Malla, said he saved his mother by pulling her hand. He said he had given his phone to his sister so she could keep in touch, but the mobile was no longer reachable. "I am worried she must be swept away." Another woman, Goma Pandit, said she had lost her buffaloes and all her other cattle. "My farmland is also swept away. Ten sacks of mustard seeds, tons of corn and rice paddy are all gone. Nothing is left." At Kathmandu's TU Teaching Hospital, families of those missing in the floods wait anxiously for updates. Holding up her phone, Ram Khumari Shrestha says: "This is my husband. He was off to Rasuwa as a part of his driving job. He was in contact with me until 8 pm yesterday. "But I couldn't call him this morning. The phone was switched off," she told the BBC. Mani Shrestha Bishwa was also camped out at the hospital on Wednesday night, hoping to hear from his younger brother, cousin, uncle and friend. "I last contacted them at 8:30 in the morning," he said. Trekking guide Sonam Dorjee missed the flood in his home village of Rasiwa Syafru by about an hour. He had left at 08:00 local time. As he was driving to Kathmandu, Dorjee told the BBC he had heard the sound of floods gushing into their village. "It [sounded] like an earthquake," he said. "My house has collapsed... I have seen a photo." Dorjee said his sister, Dechen Tamang, was missing, along with her husband and several other family members. He described the flood as "sudden and devastating". "Many survivors are now left without homes and they need emergency rescue and evacuation, as well as food, temporary accommodation and medical support." He is praying his sister is found alive. "There is a 10% chance, we hope," he said. Related topics - Published1 hour ago

item.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd948kn02e5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods - Published Devastating landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead and thousands more missing. At least 579 people have been killed and nearly 2,000 people remain unaccounted for, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. At least five people have died in Tibet, with another 558 reported missing by Chinese state media. On Wednesday, flood water tore through the border region, sweeping away homes and roads, local officials have said. Rescue workers say they now face a critical moment to reach remaining survivors as fears mount of further flooding in the disaster's aftermath. Here is what we know so far. What caused the landslide? Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating floods early on Wednesday. However, the US Geological Survey (USGS) later confirmed that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse" - when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates. The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to the agency, causing "subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream". Powerful flood water and debris travelled some 62 miles (100km) downstream from the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi Rivers, the USGS said, sweeping through towns popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims in northern Nepal. Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles as people fled in the Nuwakot region. In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuwagadhi Border checkpoint, a multi-storey building on the Nepalese side. Gyirong Port, over the border, was also hit. A number of deaths were reported in Tibetan villages. Scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events as rescue efforts continue. Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet. "I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, [which] dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood," he told the BBC. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of debris that washed into the river systems. The ICIDMOD said it was assessing whether the Trishuli River had been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If this is the case, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam and a second flood. Separately, China has warned there was a "high risk" a lake that formed after the landslide may burst its banks, causing fresh flooding downstream. As of Friday, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated, according to broadcaster CCTV. State media reported that rescue operations were briefly suspended on Friday after the lake, which has formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, overflowed - before water levels dropped slightly. Heavy rain is forecast over the next few days. But experts have told the BBC that it was possible that the lake could drain naturally over time. How many people are dead and missing? The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear. At least 579 people had died as of Friday, according to Nepali police, while the country's disaster agency said at least 1,924 people were still missing. The government has released a list of more than 517 foreign nationals who have been out of contact since the floods hit, including 33 UK nationals. The missing also include 44 members of the Nepali army and 28 police officers, disaster officials have said. Meanwhile, five people have died in Tibet and 558 are missing, China's state broadcaster CCTV reports. These figures have not been independently verified. Tibet, which China annexed in the 1950s, is one of the most strictly controlled regions in the country. It is virtually impossible for foreign media to gain entry there and trying to contact local residents is just as hard. It is unclear whether any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice. Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, a spokesman for Nepal's army, told the BBC that rain and unpredictable weather in the area were making rescue operations increasingly challenging. Which countries are the missing tourists from? Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Reports of those missing include the following: - India - at least 320 Indian nationals are missing, the foreing ministry in Delhi says - China - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in Nepal - US - 90 Americans are still missing, the US state department says - Ukraine - 62 Ukrainian nationals are missing, Nepalese police say - Malaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials say - Australia - Australia's foreign minister says 39 Australians are among the missing and there's an "unfortunate possibility" the number will rise - UK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missing - Canada - 30 Canadians and permanent residents are missing, says Global Affairs Canada Smaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand are also among the missing. How are governments responding? As rescue operations continued on Friday, the office of Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said "additional" personnel were on the ground to speed up recovery efforts. It added that a 1,200-strong team has been deployed "along the riverbanks from Rasuwa to Chitwan" and "to all possible locations along the affected areas". Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting of officials to co-ordinate rescue efforts, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua. Kamal Kishore, special representative of the UN secretary general for disaster risk reduction, urged countries to support response efforts. The US previously promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid for communities affected by the floods, while the UK said it had offered £5m. Meanwhile, the Indian Air Force said that military cargo planes carrying nearly 50 tonnes of supplies had been sent to Nepal. Might climate change have played a role? Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. Geologist Daniel Shugar – one of the first experts to suggest Wednesday's flash flooding could have been caused by glacial activity – said glacial thinning caused by global warming could increase the risk of landslides. But it is still too early to definitively link the event to climate change, Shugar, who is based at the University of Calgary in Canada, told the BBC. Simon Cook, a geoscientist at the University of Dundee, said that climate change "could have an impact". He said his team believed they had identified where the collapse had occurred. He told the BBC that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - approximately 15km west of the site of the floods - had collapsed. Cook estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream. He told the BBC that "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides". - Published10 hours ago
